Malrotation with midgut volvulus is the most urgent consideration—bilious emesis is often the first and only sign before ischemia or perforation; it carries high mortality if missed, hence highest confidence (0.95). Duodenal atresia commonly presents with bilious vomiting (though sometimes non-bilious if proximal to ampulla) and polyhydramnios history; classic 'double bubble' on X-ray makes it highly plausible (0.88). Jejunoileal atresia typically causes bilious vomiting and abdominal distension later in first 24–48h, but can present at birth with severe forms (0.75). Meconium ileus—strongly associated with cystic fibrosis—presents with bilious vomiting, failure to pass meconium, and often a 'ground-glass' or soap-bubble appearance on X-ray; high pretest probability in appropriate ethnic/clinical context (0.72). Hirschsprung disease rarely presents neonatally with bilious vomiting (usually constipation, abdominal distension, or enterocolitis), but total colonic aganglionosis may mimic high obstruction and cause bilious emesis; less common and usually non-bilious early on, thus lower confidence (0.62). Other entities like annular pancreas, intestinal duplication, or NEC were excluded from top 5 due to lower prevalence or inconsistent timing (e.g., NEC typically after 24–48h)."}

Duodenal atresia is the most common cause of proximal obstruction presenting with bilious vomiting and often associated with polyhydramnios and Down syndrome; its classic imaging finding (double-bubble sign) and high pretest probability warrant top confidence. Malrotation with volvulus is a surgical emergency—bilious vomiting is often the only early sign, and delay risks bowel necrosis; though meconium passage history is unknown, its acuity and life-threatening nature justify high confidence. Meconium ileus (strongly associated with cystic fibrosis) presents with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium—or passage of abnormally thick, inspissated meconium; absence of specified meconium details lowers confidence slightly but not substantially. Jejunoileal atresia typically causes distal obstruction with later onset of bilious vomiting and variable meconium passage; earlier presentation is less typical but possible, hence moderate confidence. Hirschsprung disease usually presents with delayed meconium passage (>48h) and progressive distension; isolated bilious vomiting without distension is atypical, and total colonic involvement is rare (<5% of cases), making it the least likely of the top five—but still plausible given the nonspecific early presentation and potential for proximal backup causing bilious reflux."}
